Resurrection Body
rĕz-ŭ-rĕk´shŭn bŏd´y
n. phrase (the glorified body the redeemed receive at Christ's coming — the same body raised, transformed and made immortal)
Latin resurgere, to rise again. The doctrine is the church's answer to the Greek hope of a soul escaping the body: Christianity's hope is a body raised, and the creed says so in as many words.

Biblical Definition

The resurrection body is the believer's own body, raised and glorified. Paul sets out four contrasts: “It is sown in corruption; it is raised in incorruption: it is sown in dishonour; it is raised in glory: it is sown in weakness; it is raised in power: it is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body” (1Co 15:42–44). The change is necessary: “this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality” (1Co 15:53). The pattern is Christ's: He “shall change our vile body, that it may be fashioned like unto his glorious body” (Php 3:21). The likeness is promised: “we shall be like him; for we shall see him as he is” (1Jn 3:2). And His own risen body was handled: “a spirit hath not flesh and bones, as ye see me have” (Luk 24:39).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines resurrection as a rising again, particularly the revival of the dead of the human race, or their return from the grave, particularly at the general judgment.

expand to see more

RESURRECTION, n. A rising again; the revival of the dead of the human race, or their return from the grave, particularly at the general judgment.

By the resurrection of Christ we have assurance of the future resurrection of men. 1 Cor. 15.

IMMORTALITY, n. The quality of never ceasing to live or exist; exemption from death and annihilation; life destined to endure without end.

Key Scripture

1Co 15:42 — "So also is the resurrection of the dead. It is sown in corruption; it is raised in incorruption:"

1Co 15:44 — "It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body. There is a natural body, and there is a spiritual body."

1Co 15:53 — "For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality."

Php 3:21 — "Who shall change our vile body, that it may be fashioned like unto his glorious body, according to the working whereby he is able even to subdue all things unto himself."

1Jn 3:2 — "Beloved, now are we the sons of God, and it doth not yet appear what we shall be: but we know that, when he shall appear, we shall be like him; for we shall see him as he is."

Modern Corruption

“Spiritual body” is read as a body made of spirit, and Paul uses the same adjective in the same letter of ordinary Christians.

expand to see more

The decisive misreading is of one adjective. Paul contrasts a natural body (psuchikos, soulish) with a spiritual body (pneumatikos), and neither word names a material. He uses the same pair in chapter two for the natural man and the spiritual man, where nobody imagines the spiritual man is made of vapour. The adjective describes what animates and governs a thing. The resurrection body is a real body wholly under the Spirit's rule — incorruptible, glorious, powerful — and the whole force of the chapter is that it is this body, sown and raised, rather than a replacement issued at the graveside.

That is why Luke 24:39 is doctrine and not merely narrative. The disciples supposed they had seen a spirit, and the Lord answered with the most physical demonstration available: handle me and see, for a spirit hath not flesh and bones, as ye see me have — and then He ate a piece of broiled fish in front of them. He showed them the wounds. Whatever glorification did to that body, it did not remove it, and He has not laid it down since; there is a Man in heaven.

The practical consequence reaches into how Christians grieve and how they live. A funeral consoled entirely by the soul's release has borrowed from Plato, and 1 Corinthians 15 offers something better and stranger: the body in the ground is a seed, and what is sown is what comes up. It also settles ethics. If the body is destined for glory, then what is done in it matters permanently, chronic illness is not the last word on a life, and the care of a dying person's body is not a low task. First John 3:2 supplies the one detail that outranks all the others: it doth not yet appear what we shall be, but we shall be like him.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek anastasis (G386), resurrection; psuchikos / pneumatikos (G5591, G4152), natural / spiritual; aphtharsia (G861), incorruption; metaschematizo (G3345), to change the fashion of.

expand to see more

Greek anastasis (G386) — resurrection, a standing up again; 1 Corinthians 15:42, John 11:25, Acts 17:32, Philippians 3:10.

Greek psuchikos / pneumatikos (G5591, G4152) — natural / spiritual; 1 Corinthians 15:44–46, and of men, 2:14–15.

Greek metaschematisei (G3345) — shall change the fashion of; Philippians 3:21.

Usage

"“Sown in corruption… raised in incorruption” — the same thing, sown and raised."

"“A spirit hath not flesh and bones, as ye see me have” — and then He ate."

"“We shall be like him; for we shall see him as he is”."
